Cas9. An RNA-guided nuclease from the bacterial immune system that has become a transformative gene-editing tool. Cas9 cleaves DNA at specific sequences, and unlike older techniques, it needs only a new 20-base RNA guide for each new target rather than extensive protein engineering. It catalyzes double-strand DNA breaks about three to four base pairs upstream of a PAM—a protospacer adjacent motif, typically NGG in the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes. A synthetic 20-base RNA sequence, known as the CRISPR RNA or crRNA, directs Cas9 to its genomic target with perfect complementarity. The mechanism is elegant: Cas9 searches the DNA, unwinds it locally, and tests Watson-Crick base pairing. Only when the PAM is adjacent and the guide RNA matches does the nuclease domain become active and cut both strands. The cleavage products can be blunt or sticky ends depending on the variant, and both activate the cell's DNA repair pathways. Non-homologous end joining causes mutations and disrupts genes, while homology-directed repair can insert new sequences. Cas9's origin traces back to bacterial defense against phages, where invading DNA is incorporated as RNA guides to prevent future infection. Delivering Cas9 into cells requires viral vectors, electroporation, nanoparticles, or other methods. The technology has enabled disease modeling, functional genomics at scale, and therapeutic applications including treatments for sickle cell and beta-thalassemia now in clinical use. Ongoing refinements with high-fidelity variants, smaller orthologs from other bacteria, and prime editing further expand its capabilities and safety.
